meta.description: Real Hippocrates: Aphorisms I.6. But this exact English is the wording printed in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations from 1876 on, not a translation from the Greek.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Extreme remedies are very appropriate for extreme diseases'?
meta.ogDescription: The sentence is genuinely Hippocratic. The famous English is the one Bartlett's has printed since 1876 — Francis Adams's 1849 translation reads differently.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: c. 460 – c. 377 BC · Greek physician of Kos
answer.sourceLine: Hippocrates, Aphorisms, Section I, no. 6 — a real sentence of the Hippocratic corpus, still there in the Greek. This particular English, though, is the uncredited wording printed under his name in Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations from the tenth edition of 1876 onward — and it reads as an Englishing of the Latin school text Ad extremos morbos, extrema remedia exquisite optima, following that far more closely than any rendering made from the Greek.

source.heading: Where the line comes from

docMeta.dd: Ad extremos morbos, extrema remedia exquisite optima.
Standard English by Francis Adams, 1849; the famous wording is the uncredited one printed in Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations from 1876

source.excerpt: 6. For extreme diseases, extreme methods of cure, as to restriction, are most suitable. 7. When the disease is very acute, it is attended with extremely severe symptoms in its first stage; and therefore an extremely attenuating diet must be used. When this is not the case, but it is allowable to give a more generous diet, we may depart as far from the severity of regimen as the disease, by its mildness, is removed from the extreme.
trail: The Greek of Section I, no. 6 survives and says what the tradition says it says — “Ἐς δὲ τὰ Ἄσχατα νουσήματα αἱ Ἄσχαται θεραπεῖαι ἐς ἀκριβείην, κράτισται.” Greek Wikisource ↗

The standard English rendering is not the famous one. Francis Adams, whose 1849 translation of the Aphorisms is the version usually reprinted, gives “For extreme diseases, extreme methods of cure, as to restriction, are most suitable.” Wikisource ↗

The popular wording is Bartlett’s, and it enters in 1876. Under the heading HIPPOCRATES, after “Life is short and the art long,” Familiar Quotations prints “Extreme remedies are very appropriate for extreme diseases” and credits it only to “ibid.” — Aphorism i. No translator is named. Its earliest appearance is p. 599 of the tenth edition (Boston: Little, Brown, 1876; copyright entered 1875), where the footnote points to Shakespeare alone. It is in no earlier Bartlett we can find — the 1860 and 1868 editions and the 1870–74 reprints of the fifth and sixth carry no Hippocrates entry at all, only a footnote to Longfellow. It survives at p. 700 of the 1892 printing, which is where the Montaigne cross-reference is added, and p. 886 of the 1914 one. Familiar Quotations, 1876 ↗

The wording reads as the Latin rather than the Greek. Thomas Coar’s 1822 edition prints all three side by side: the Greek, then Ad extremos morbos, extrema remedia exquisite optima, then his own English — “In very acute diseases, because of their severity, the most active measures are the best.” No source we have found names Bartlett’s translator, so the descent cannot be documented; but the sentence reads as that Latin line put straight into English, and it tracks it far more closely than the renderings made from the Greek, which give “methods of cure” or “most active measures” and keep ἐς ἀκριβείην. That comparison is ours, not a finding we are quoting. Coar, 1822 ↗
source.cutTag: Aphorisms, Section I, nos. 6–7 · trans. Francis Adams, 1849
source.excerptNote: Adams’s “as to restriction” is carrying the Greek ἐς ἀκριβείην — strictness, exactness. Aphorism 6 sits in a run (4, 5, 7, 8) entirely about how spare a patient’s diet should be, so the “extreme remedy” in view is an extremely restricted regimen, not a drastic intervention.

source.rightsNote: The Greek original is ancient and long out of copyright. Both English wordings shown here come from pre-1931 United States or British publications — Francis Adams’s translation of 1849 and the rendering printed in Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations (Boston: Little, Brown, 1876) — so both are in the public domain in the US. A modern translation of the same aphorism would not be: rights attach to the particular English, not to Hippocrates.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.heading: Hippocrates of Kos
author.metaLine: c. 460 – c. 377 BC · Greek physician of Kos, the father of medicine
author.bio: Hippocrates was a physician of the island of Kos whose name became the banner for a large body of Greek medical writing — the Hippocratic corpus — only some of which he plausibly wrote himself. The Aphorisms are the most quoted part of it: several hundred terse clinical rules, opening with the one everybody knows, “Life is short, and Art long.” Because the corpus is anonymous in places and enormously famous everywhere, Hippocrates has become a magnet for invented medical wisdom — which makes it worth saying clearly when a line, like this one, is actually his.

misattribution.heading: What actually gets said wrong
misattribution.intro: Hippocrates is one of the internet’s great fake-quote magnets — “Let food be thy medicine” and “Walking is man’s best medicine” both sit in Wikiquote’s Disputed section ↗. This one is different. The sentence is real; what travels is a wording he never wrote and a meaning he did not intend.

items.why: Hippocrates wrote Greek, and no one records who made this English. On our reading it follows the Latin school text far more closely than any Greek-based rendering does — Ad extremos morbos, extrema remedia exquisite optima, printed opposite the Greek in Thomas Coar’s 1822 Aphorisms ↗. Coar’s own English of the same line reads “In very acute diseases, because of their severity, the most active measures are the best.”

items.who: Anyone reading it as ‘desperate times, desperate measures’
items.why: In Francis Adams’s 1849 translation ↗ the qualifier survives — “extreme methods of cure, as to restriction” — and the aphorism sits among nos. 4, 5, 7 and 8, all of which are about how thin a sick person’s diet should be. Strip the qualifier and a rule about starving a fever becomes a general licence for drastic action.

Bartlett’s own footnote to the line points the reader to Shakespeare and to Montaigne’s “For a desperate disease a desperate cure” — Familiar Quotations, 1892, p. 700 ↗. Wikiquote extends the same comparison list to Hamlet Act iv, Sc. 3, Guy Fawkes on the Gunpowder Plot, and Dryden. Those are echoes and analogues, not sources for this sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Hippocrates — Aphorisms, Section I, no. 6, still legible in the Greek ↗. The famous English sentence, though, belongs to a translator, and it was Bartlett’s that made it famous.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The Aphorisms were the most memorised medical text in Europe for something close to two thousand years, and for most of that time they were memorised in Latin, not Greek. That is how a compressed Greek rule about dietary strictness came out the other end as a crisp English maxim about drastic cures — each stage of translation shaving off a little more of the clinical setting until only the rhetoric was left.

It is a useful case precisely because nothing was faked. Nobody invented a Hippocrates quote here; a real one simply drifted, and the drift is documented at every step: the Greek, the Latin gloss, the free 19th-century renderings, and finally the quotation dictionary that fixed one wording in place.
context.detailsSummary: Three centuries of the same aphorism, in three Englishes
detailsBody: 1817 — an edition built on the Latin version of Verhoofd prints Ad extremos morbos, extrema remedia exquisite optima and renders it loosely on the facing page as “The greater the evil — the more vigorous the remedy.” Internet Archive ↗
1822 — Thomas Coar sets Greek, Latin and English in parallel and translates: “In very acute diseases, because of their severity, the most active measures are the best.” Internet Archive ↗
1849 — Francis Adams, still the most reprinted English Aphorisms, keeps the qualifier: “For extreme diseases, extreme methods of cure, as to restriction, are most suitable.” Wikisource ↗

1876 — Bartlett’s tenth edition prints, on p. 599, the version everyone now quotes, with no translator credited and no qualifier left. It was in none of the earlier editions, which have no Hippocrates entry; the 1892 printing carries it on to p. 700. Internet Archive ↗
context.pull: The ‘extreme remedy’ he meant was an extremely spare diet.

sourcesVerified.claim: Greek Wikisource's text of Aphorisms Section I gives no. 6 as: Ἐς δὲ τὰ ἔσχατα νουσήματα αἱ ἔσχαται θεραπεῖαι ἐς ἀκριβείην, κράτισται.

English Wikisource hosts the Aphorisms with header 'translator = Francis Adams' and note 'Translated in 1849'; Section 1, no. 6 reads 'For extreme diseases, extreme methods of cure, as to restriction, are most suitable.' and nos. 4, 5, 7 and 8 concern spare/restricted diet.

Wikiquote's Hippocrates page, in its sourced Aphorisms section, gives 1:6 as 'For extreme diseases, extreme methods of cure, as to restriction, are most suitable.' with the variant translation 'Extreme remedies are very appropriate for extreme diseases.' and compares Guy Fawkes, Shakespeare's Hamlet Act iv Sc. 3, Montaigne and Dryden; its separate Disputed section lists 'Let food be thy medicine' and 'Walking is man's best medicine'. The page dates Hippocrates c. 460 BC - 377 BC.

Bartlett's Familiar Quotations (Boston: Little, Brown, 1892; copyright 1875, 1882, 1891) prints on p. 700 under HIPPOCRATES: 'Life is short and the art long. Aphorism i.' and 'Extreme remedies are very appropriate for extreme diseases. ibid.', with a footnote reading 'See Shakespeare, page 141.' and 'For a desperate disease a desperate cure. — Montaigne: Chap. iii. The Custom of the Isle of Cea.' No translator is credited for the Hippocrates entries.

Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, Tenth Edition (Boston: Little, Brown, 1876; 'Entered according to act of Congress, in the year 1875, by John Bartlett') already prints on p. 599, under HIPPOCRATES: 'Life is short and the art long. Aphorism i.' and 'Extreme remedies are very appropriate for extreme diseases.* ibid.', the footnote reading only 'Diseases, desperate grown, By desperate appliance are relieved. Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act iv. Sc. 3.' — no Montaigne, and no translator credited. This is the earliest Bartlett appearance found: the 1870, 1871, 1872 and 1874 reprints of the fifth and sixth editions (1868 copyright) contain no occurrence of 'extreme remedies' and mention Hippocrates only in a footnote to Longfellow's 'Ars longa, vita brevis'.
The 1914 Little, Brown printing of Bartlett's Familiar Quotations carries the same Hippocrates entry, including 'Extreme remedies are very appropriate for extreme diseases', on p. 886.

Thomas Coar's 'The Aphorisms of Hippocrates: with a Translation into Latin, and English' (London: A. J. Valpy, MDCCCXXII) prints aphorism VI in Greek, then the Latin 'Ad extremos morbos, extrema remedia exquisite optima.', then Coar's English 'In very acute diseases, because of their severity, the most active measures are the best.'

An 1817 edition, 'The Aphorisms of Hippocrates, from the Latin version of Verhoofd, with a literal translation on the opposite page', prints aphorism 6 as Latin 'Ad extremos morbos, extrema remedia exquisite optima.' with the facing English 'The greater the evil — the more vigorous the remedy.'
Quote Investigator's own site search for 'desperate diseases desperate remedies' returns 'Nothing Found' — QI has no article on this quote, so there is no anchor conclusion to defer to.
